The Distributive Law

ArithmeticCounting
Game: A block of squares is cut into smaller blocks until only single squares are left, and each cut rewrites the multiplication as an addition; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Press in a gap between two columns or two rows to cut there. With the keyboard, move the marked square with the arrow keys and press C or R.

Press in a gap to cut. Arrow keys move the marked square; C cuts after its column, R below its row.

    <
    Look for the math

    Multiplying counting numbers is counting in equal groups: 4×5 is four groups of five. The distributive law says that if you split each group of five into two and three, you have four twos and four threes.

    One cut, one identity

    A cut between two columns turns a×(b+c) into a×b + a×c, because the b+c columns of the block become two blocks of b and c columns, each still a rows high. A cut between rows does the same to the other factor: (a+b)×c = a×c + b×c.

    Cut it all the way

    Keep cutting and every piece ends as a single square, written 1. Whatever the order of the cuts, the block of N×M squares takes exactly N×M − 1 cuts, because each cut adds one piece and you start with one. The logic test tried every cutting order on every board up to 3 by 3 and 400 random orders on boards up to 12 by 12; the written sum always added up to the right product.

    Not a proof

    The page says plainly that counting squares is no proof: whether the law holds depends on the axioms for numbers you start from (Landau’s Foundations of Analysis derives it for whole, rational, real and complex numbers). It is a picture of why the law is believable for counting numbers.

    Cut a 4 by 5 block once after the second column, then cut the pieces again below the second row. How many products are in the sum, and what do they add to?
